cases.prompt:
Advisory only - do not use any tools; answer from reasoning alone, on stdout. Review the design below. Several sections have minor issues; exactly one section has a flaw that can cause direct financial harm to customers and must be fixed before launch. Which section is it?

Design: card payments service (payhub)

§1 Naming. The service is called payhub-svc. Its endpoints mix styles: POST /createCharge and POST /refund_charge.

§2 Logging. Every request logs one INFO line with method, path, status and latency. Volume is about 2 GB a day, a little more than the team needs.

§3 Audit table. Each charge writes one row to audit_events. The table is read only by a monthly compliance export, which has no index on created_at and takes about 40 seconds.

§4 Retries. The charge worker calls the payment processor's POST /charges with an Idempotency-Key header. The processor deduplicates requests that carry the same key. On a timeout or a 5xx the worker retries up to 3 times, and every attempt, including each retry, generates a fresh UUIDv4 as its Idempotency-Key.

§5 Settlement. A nightly job downloads the processor's settlement file and matches each settled charge to the charges table by the processor's charge id; unmatched rows go to a review queue.

§6 Monitoring. Dashboards show p95 latency and error rate; an alert fires when the error rate stays above 2% for 5 minutes.

Reason briefly, then end with exactly one line naming that section in the form FLAW: §N (for example FLAW: §2)
cases.note: Three decoys (§1 naming, §2 log volume, §3 missing index on a cold table); §4 mints a new idempotency key per retry, so a timeout retry double-charges.

cases.prompt:
Advisory only - do not use any tools; answer from reasoning alone, on stdout. A team is deciding whether to split its monolith into microservices. The facts:
- The team is 4 engineers.
- They deploy once a week, and nobody has asked for more often.
- Every feature reads and writes one shared Postgres database.
- p95 latency is 80 ms against a 200 ms target.
- There is no on-call rotation.

Candidate arguments:
A. Four engineers cannot own, deploy and monitor several services; the operational load per person would multiply.
B. Separate services can scale independently when one feature gets heavy load.
C. Latency is already over its target, and extra network hops would push it further out of bounds.
D. All features share one database, so split services would stay coupled through the schema: a distributed monolith.
E. Separate services let each team deploy independently, many times a day.
F. With no on-call rotation, more moving parts means more failures that nobody is paged for.

You are assigned to argue AGAINST splitting. Pick the three arguments you would use: each must argue against splitting AND be consistent with the facts. Reason briefly, then end with exactly one line in the form ARGS: X,Y,Z
cases.note: Stance plus grounding, not rhetoric: B and E argue for splitting, C contradicts the latency fact.
